title: School should start later
text: High schools should start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Teenagers naturally fall asleep and wake up later than children or adults, so a 7:15 bell asks them to learn while their bodies still think it is night. A 2014 study of 9,000 students in three states found that schools that moved their start time later saw higher attendance and fewer car accidents among teen drivers. Critics say later schedules hurt sports and after-school jobs. Those problems are real, but they can be solved with lights and flexible shifts. Sleep is not a luxury for a growing brain.

title: Homework in elementary school
text: Elementary schools give too much homework. A seven-year-old who has been in class for six hours needs to play, eat dinner with family, and sleep. Research summarized by Harris Cooper found almost no link between homework and achievement before middle school. What homework does teach young children is that learning is a chore. I would replace worksheets with twenty minutes of reading for fun. Parents could then spend evenings talking with their kids instead of fighting over fractions.

title: Uniforms
text: Some people believe school uniforms fix everything, from bullying to bad grades. They do not. Uniforms cost families an average of 150 dollars a year, and students still find ways to compare shoes and backpacks. The best case for uniforms is that mornings get easier, which is true but small. If a school wants less bullying, it should hire more counselors, not more tailors.

title: Social media and teenagers
text: Social media is not simply good or bad for teenagers, but the way most apps are built pushes it toward bad. Endless scrolling and like counters are designed to keep users on the screen as long as possible. In a survey by the Pew Research Center, 46 percent of teens said they are online almost constantly. Many of them also reported feeling worse about their bodies and friendships afterward. Platforms should be required to turn off autoplay and hide like counts for users under 16. Teens deserve tools that help them put the phone down.

title: Working from home
text: Remote work should be the default for jobs that can be done on a laptop. Commuting wastes about an hour a day for the average American worker, which adds up to more than 200 hours a year. Companies that allow remote work also see lower turnover. Some managers argue that creativity needs people in the same room. Maybe so, but a company can bring teams together four times a year without forcing everyone to sit in traffic every morning.

title: The four-day work week
text: A four-day work week is worth trying. In a 2022 trial in the United Kingdom, 61 companies cut the work week to four days with no loss of pay, and 56 of them kept the schedule afterward. Workers reported less burnout, and revenue stayed about the same. The fear that people would simply do less turned out to be wrong, because they worked more carefully when their time was limited.

title: Banning plastic bags
text: Cities should ban single-use plastic bags. A plastic bag is used for about twelve minutes and then lasts for hundreds of years in a landfill or a river. When Ireland charged a small fee, bag use dropped by over 90 percent in a year. People did not suffer; they just bought a reusable bag. A small habit change, repeated by millions, protects wildlife and keeps our streets cleaner.

title: Zoos
text: Zoos have a place, but only if they put animals first. Accredited zoos have helped save species such as the California condor and the golden lion tamarin from extinction. At the same time, a small cage cannot give an elephant the space it needs, and many elephants in zoos die young. I would keep zoos that run real breeding and rescue programs, and close the ones that exist only for entertainment.

title: Free college
text: Public colleges should be free. Student loan debt in the United States is now over 1.7 trillion dollars, and it holds back a whole generation from buying homes and starting businesses. A free degree would cost taxpayers money, yes, but educated workers earn more and pay more taxes for decades. Countries like Germany already offer free tuition and have not collapsed. If we call education the ladder to opportunity, we should not charge people to stand on the first step.

title: Violent video games
text: Violent video games are blamed for far more than they deserve. Millions of people play shooting games and never hurt anyone, and crime rates fell in the years when games became more realistic. The American Psychological Association has said there is no clear proof that games cause real violence. Parents should still check ratings for young children, but it is lazy to use a game as an excuse when the real causes of violence are much more complicated.

title: Lowering the voting age
text: Sixteen-year-olds should be allowed to vote. They pay taxes on their jobs, they can be tried as adults, and they will live longest with the results of today's decisions about climate and education. Austria lowered its voting age to 16 in 2007, and young voters there turned out at higher rates than slightly older first-time voters. Giving teens the vote early builds a lifelong habit of taking part.

title: Free public transport
text: Making buses and trains free would be one of the cheapest ways to help a city. Fares often cover less than a third of the real cost of running transit, so the money lost is smaller than people think. Free rides would cut traffic and pollution and help low-income workers reach jobs. The city of Tallinn made transport free for residents in 2013, and ridership rose. It is a small change with big benefits for everyone.

title: Teaching cursive
text: Schools should still teach cursive handwriting. Some say it is outdated because everyone types now. But writing by hand uses different parts of the brain, and studies suggest students remember notes better when they write them. Cursive also lets people read old letters and historical documents, such as the Constitution. It takes only a few weeks to learn, which is a very small price for a useful skill.

title: Funding space exploration
text: Space exploration is worth its cost. NASA's budget is less than half of one percent of all federal spending, and it has given us GPS technology, better water filters, and weather satellites that warn us before hurricanes. Beyond the inventions, there is something I believe in strongly: humans need big goals that unite them. Landing on Mars will inspire a generation of scientists the way the moon landing did.

title: A tax on junk food
text: A tax on sugary drinks and junk food is reasonable. When Mexico taxed soda at one peso a litre in 2014, purchases fell by about 6 percent in the first year, and fell more among poorer households. The money can pay for school lunches and clinics. Opponents call it nanny-state interference, but we already tax cigarettes for the same reason: the product harms health and the public pays the bill.

title: Animal testing
text: Animal testing is a painful tradition that we are slowly learning to leave behind. Many drugs that work in mice fail in humans, so the tests are not even reliable. New methods, such as organs grown on small chips and computer models, can give better answers without hurting any animal. Until those methods are ready for every medicine, testing should be allowed only when there is no alternative, and with strict rules against needless suffering.

title: Nuclear energy
text: If we are serious about climate change, we must keep and build nuclear power plants. Nuclear produces almost no carbon dioxide and runs day and night, unlike wind and solar, which depend on weather. Accidents like Chernobyl scare people, yet statistically nuclear power has caused fewer deaths per unit of energy than coal. Waste storage is a challenge, but a manageable one. Refusing nuclear power means burning more fossil fuel, which is the greater danger.

title: Standardized tests
text: Standardized tests measure how well students take tests, and little else. A single Saturday morning cannot capture a student's curiosity, creativity, or persistence. Many colleges, including the University of Chicago, have stopped requiring test scores and have still admitted strong classes. Teachers also complain that they spend weeks teaching to the test instead of teaching to the student. Grades, projects, and recommendations give a fuller picture of who someone is.

title: Phones in classrooms
text: Students should keep phones in their lockers during lessons. A phone buzzing in a pocket pulls attention away even when nobody touches it. One study from the University of Texas found that students scored lower on tests when their phones were merely on the desk. Teachers should be allowed to make exceptions for projects, but the default must be off. School is one of the few places left where people can think without interruption.

title: Art and music classes
text: Cutting art and music classes to save money is a mistake. These subjects teach teamwork, patience, and creative problem solving, which employers say they want. For many students, the band room or art studio is the reason they come to school at all. Schools that cut the arts often save only a tiny part of the budget, yet the loss is felt for years. Let us treat the arts as basic, not as extras.

title: Raising the minimum wage
text: The federal minimum wage has been stuck at 7.25 dollars since 2009, which means a full-time worker earns less than 15,000 dollars a year before taxes. No one can rent an apartment on that. Economists disagree on how much job loss a higher wage would cause, but most studies of recent increases found little effect. I believe a worker who gives a full day of labor deserves enough to live on, and the law should say so.

title: Fast fashion
text: Fast fashion is cheap for buyers and expensive for the planet. The industry produces about 10 percent of global carbon emissions, and a truckload of clothing is burned or dumped every second. Shirts that cost five dollars are made by workers paid very little, in factories that are sometimes unsafe. Shoppers can help by buying fewer, better pieces and by trading used clothes. Companies should also be forced to report where and how their goods are made.

title: Are e-sports real sports?
text: E-sports deserve to be called sports. Professional players train for hours each day, practise strict teamwork, and need reflexes that are measured in milliseconds. In 2019 the League of Legends world final was watched by more than 100 million people, more than many traditional championships. Skeptics point out that there is no running involved. But chess and shooting are sports too, and no one doubts their skill.

title: Ending daylight saving time
text: We should stop changing the clocks twice a year. The spring shift costs everyone an hour of sleep, and studies have linked it to a short rise in heart attacks and traffic crashes the following Monday. Farmers, who were supposed to benefit, mostly dislike it. Pick one time, standard time, and keep it. It would be a rare law that everybody could agree makes life simpler.

title: Why libraries still matter
text: Libraries are more than rooms full of books. They offer free internet, job help, language classes, and a warm place to sit for people who have nowhere else. In many small towns the library is the only public space left. Some leaders want to cut library hours to balance budgets, which saves little and hurts a lot. A town that closes its library is deciding that some of its citizens do not count.

title: The day Biscuit got lost
text: Biscuit slipped out of the gate on a Tuesday afternoon, and by dinner my mother was calling his name from the porch. I walked every street in our neighbourhood with a flashlight and a handful of dog treats, feeling more scared with every block. Just before nine I heard a jingle behind the bakery. He was sitting beside the back door, wet and proud, with a bread roll in his mouth. I carried him home and did not put him down until morning.

title: First day in a new city
text: The boxes were still stacked in the hallway when I walked into my new school. Everyone seemed to know where to sit, and I stood by the door holding a schedule I could not read. A girl with bright red sneakers looked up and said, 'You can sit here.' That was all. I remember how small those words were and how large they felt. By lunch I knew her name was Priya, and the city did not feel quite so big.

title: My grandmother's kitchen
text: My grandmother's kitchen always smelled like cardamom and onions frying in butter. She never used a recipe. 'Your hands will know,' she would say, pushing flour toward me across the table. I made a lopsided dumpling, and she ate it anyway, smiling as if it were perfect. She passed away last winter. Last week I made her curry from memory, and when I tasted it I was suddenly ten years old again, standing on a stool beside her.

title: Failing my driving test
text: I knew I had failed before the examiner finished writing. I had rolled through a stop sign while thinking about whether my hands were at ten and two. Back in the parking lot my father said nothing for a long minute, then handed me a cold drink. 'I failed twice,' he said. I had never heard that before. We drove home with me still behind the wheel, and I passed the following month.

title: The championship game
text: With two minutes left we were down by one goal, and my legs felt like wet sand. Coach shouted something I could not hear. The ball bounced toward me off a defender's shin, and for a moment the whole field went quiet. I kicked it without thinking. It curved past the keeper and hit the net, and the bench exploded. We lost in extra time. Strangely, I still remember that one kick better than the score.

title: The night the power went out
text: The storm took our electricity at about seven. My little brother cried until my father lit a candle and began telling us the story of the time he got lost in a cornfield. We sat on the living room floor in blankets. Nobody looked at a screen. When the lights finally flickered back on near midnight, we groaned together, because it meant the evening was over.

title: Learning to swim
text: I was eleven years old and afraid of water deeper than my knees. Every Saturday I stood at the edge of the pool in a pair of borrowed goggles while the other kids splashed past me. My instructor, a patient man named Mr. Ortega, never pushed. One morning I simply let go of the wall. I sank, kicked, and rose, gasping and laughing. It was only four metres across, but it felt like crossing an ocean.

title: The broken violin
text: I dropped my violin on the stone steps outside the music hall. The neck cracked with a sound I can still hear. For weeks I refused to touch the case. Then my teacher put an old, scratched instrument in my hands and asked me to play anything at all. The tone was rough, but it was mine. I realised that I loved the music, not the shiny wood.

title: My first job at the bakery
text: At fifteen I started at the corner bakery, where my shift began at five in the morning. My hands burned from the trays, and I mixed up the orders of the first three customers. The owner, Mrs. Alvarez, laughed gently and gave me a warm croissant. 'Everyone burns the first week,' she said. By spring I could box a dozen pastries with my eyes half closed, and I had learned that being on time can be a kind of pride.

title: Waiting at the hospital
text: We waited eleven hours in a room with a humming vending machine and a clock that seemed to run backward. My aunt knitted without looking at her hands. I read the same page of a magazine five times. When the nurse finally came through the door, she smiled before she spoke, and I felt my shoulders drop for the first time all day. My cousin was born at 3:12 in the morning.

title: The wallet
text: I found a brown leather wallet under a bench at the bus station. Inside were forty dollars, a library card, and a photo of a little boy in a yellow raincoat. I could have kept the cash. Instead I walked to the ticket window and handed it over. Two days later a letter arrived at my house with a thank-you and a drawing of a bus, signed with a crooked name in green crayon.

title: A rainy bus ride
text: The bus was packed and smelled of wet coats. I stood in the aisle gripping a pole as the windows fogged up. An old man in front of me offered me his seat, which was funny, because I was about to offer him mine. We laughed, and neither of us sat. For the next ten stops we talked about his garden, and when he got off he waved at me through the glass like an old friend.

title: My brother's wedding
text: My brother stood at the end of the aisle shaking so hard that his flower fell off his jacket. When the music started, I saw tears in his eyes before his bride even appeared. I was supposed to give a speech, but the paper in my hand went blurry. So I said only that he had always been the one who looked after me, and now someone would look after him. People clapped, and my brother hugged me too tightly to speak.

title: Camping in the storm
text: We pitched the tent just before the clouds turned black. Thunder rolled over the lake, and rain drummed on the nylon so loudly that we shouted to hear each other. Around midnight the stakes pulled loose and a corner of the tent collapsed onto my sister's face. We spent the rest of the night in the car, eating cold sandwiches and laughing until we cried. It is still our favourite trip.

title: The last box
text: The movers had gone, and only one box remained in my empty bedroom. Inside were old toys, a school medal, and a note I wrote at age nine promising to be a famous inventor. I sat on the floor and read it twice. Then I put the note in my pocket instead of the box. A new house is just walls, but I decided to carry the promise with me.

title: A letter from my best friend
text: The letter came in a blue envelope with too many stamps. Maya had moved to Canada in September, and I had been checking the mailbox every afternoon since. She wrote about snow that reached her windows and about a teacher who pronounced her name wrong. At the bottom she drew our old treehouse with a tiny flag on top. I pinned the drawing above my desk and started writing back that same night.

title: The burnt birthday cake
text: I wanted to surprise my mother with a chocolate cake, so I sneaked into the kitchen while she was at work. I forgot the timer. By the time the smoke alarm screamed, the cake looked like a black frisbee. Mom came home to open windows and a very sad kid. She cut it anyway and we scraped off the burnt parts. We ate it with ice cream, and she said it was the best cake she had ever had.

title: Walking home in the snow
text: School closed early because of the blizzard, and the buses did not come. My friend Leo and I decided to walk the three miles home. The streets were silent and white, and our footprints filled in behind us. We sang badly, threw snowballs at every stop sign, and arrived with frozen fingers and red faces. My grandmother was waiting with hot soup, and she did not scold us at all.

title: Summer on the farm
text: Every July I spent a month at my uncle's farm, getting up before the sun to feed the chickens. The first week I hated the smell and the mud. By the third week I knew every hen by name. One morning a calf was born in the barn, and my uncle let me hold the rope while it took its first wobbly steps. I went home sunburned, tired, and sorry to leave.

title: Graduation day
text: I thought I would feel proud when my name was called, but all I felt was a strange emptiness, as if a door had shut. Then I saw my parents in the crowd, my father holding up his phone and my mother wiping her eyes with a program. That was when I understood how much of this belonged to them too. I crossed the stage, shook a hand, and smiled for the camera.

title: My old red bicycle
text: My red bicycle had a bent bell and a seat held together with tape. I rode it everywhere, down the hill with no hands and along the creek to the old bridge. When I grew too tall, my father wanted to sell it. I begged him to keep it in the garage instead. Sometimes I still sit on it for a minute, the way you might visit an old friend.

title: Goodbye at the train station
text: The train was already hissing when my grandfather took my hand. He did not like speeches, so he pressed a small coin into my palm and said, 'For luck.' I wanted to say a hundred things, but only managed to nod. As the carriage pulled away I pressed my face to the window and watched him get smaller on the platform until he was just a grey coat and a lifted hand.

title: The spelling bee
text: I was in the final round, and my word was 'necessary.' My mind went completely white. The room waited. I began slowly: n, e, c, e, double s, a, r, y. The judge paused, then smiled and said it was correct. I won by one word. Afterward, my teacher told me she had been hiding behind her program the whole time because she could not bear to watch.

title: Our garage band
text: We practised in Dev's garage every Friday, with a drum kit that was missing a cymbal and an amplifier that only worked if you kicked it. We were terrible. Our first show was at a school fundraiser, and we played four songs for about thirty people, two of whom were our mothers. When we finished, a boy in the back shouted for one more. We had only rehearsed four, so we played the first one again.

title: Thunder
text: I used to hide under my bed whenever it thundered. One night my little sister, who was five, climbed in with me and asked if I was scared. 'No,' I lied. 'Then why are you shaking?' she said. I started to laugh, and she did too. After that, every storm became a game where we counted seconds between the flash and the sound, and the fear slowly went away.
